title: Independent-Samples t-Test (with Worked Example)
content:
# The Independent-Samples t-Test

## What it is
An **independent-samples t-test** compares the means of **two separate groups** to ask whether the difference observed in the samples reflects a real difference between the population means (μ₁ vs μ₂), or just sampling variability. "Independent" means there is no special relationship between observations in the two groups — e.g., participants randomly assigned to one of two conditions. (If each subject contributes *two* scores, use a paired/correlated t-test instead.)

## Hypotheses
- H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ (the population means are equal; the difference is 0)
- H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (two-sided; one-sided versions are also possible)

## Assumptions
1. **Homogeneity of variance** — the two populations have the same variance.
2. **Normality** — the populations are normally distributed.
3. **Independence** — each value is sampled independently; each subject provides only one value.

Small-to-moderate violations of assumptions 1 and 2 make little difference; violating assumption 3 is serious.

## The test statistic
The general significance-testing formula is:

t = (statistic − hypothesized value) / (standard error of the statistic)

Here the statistic is the difference between sample means and the hypothesized value is 0:

t = (M₁ − M₂) / s_{M₁−M₂}

With equal variances, the standard error of the difference uses the **pooled variance** s²_p — a sample-size-weighted average of the two sample variances — and the degrees of freedom are df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. (The two samples need not be the same size; the unequal-variance alternative, Welch's test, is more complicated and reduces the degrees of freedom.)

## Worked example: the "Animal Research" study
Students rated (on a 7-point scale) whether animal research is wrong. Summary data by gender:

| Group | n | Mean | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Females | 17 | 5.353 | 2.743 |
| Males | 17 | 3.882 | 2.985 |

**Step 1 — the statistic (difference between means):**
M₁ − M₂ = 5.3529 − 3.8824 = **1.4705**. The hypothesized value is 0, so nothing is subtracted.

**Step 2 — the standard error of the difference.** Pool the variances (equal n, so a simple average):
s²_p = (2.743 + 2.985)/2 = 2.864
s_{M₁−M₂} = √(2.864 × (1/17 + 1/17)) = √(0.3369) ≈ **0.580**

**Step 3 — compute t:**
t = 1.4705 / 0.580 ≈ **2.53**, with df = 17 + 17 − 2 = **32**.

**Step 4 — decision.** A t of 2.53 with 32 df gives p ≈ .016 (two-tailed), below .05: reject H₀ and conclude that females rate animal research as more wrong than males do.

## Reporting
At minimum report t, df, and p (e.g., t(32) = 2.53, p = .016). It is good practice to also include a 95% confidence interval for the mean difference and an effect size such as Cohen's d — e.g., a write-up like: "A Student's independent samples t-test showed the difference was significant (t(31) = 2.1, p < .05, CI₉₅ = [0.2, 10.8], d = .74)." What to include depends on your audience and journal standards.

*Note: the data, assumptions, and Steps 1–2 follow Lane's Online Statistics Education (pp. 406–407); the pooled-variance/df framework is from Introductory Business Statistics §5.4; the reporting guidance and example stat block are from Learning Statistics with jamovi §11.4.1. The t and p values in Steps 3–4 are computed from those givens.*
